sources.publisher: Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India

passages.title: A new GDP base year changes the measuring lens
passages.text:
On 27 February 2026, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation released a new series of annual and quarterly national accounts estimates with 2022–23 as the base year, replacing the earlier 2011–12 base. A base-year revision is a regular part of national accounting. It does not mean that the economy itself has suddenly changed on the date of publication. It means that the statistical framework used to express prices, weights and economic activity has been updated to reflect a more recent structure.

The base year matters because an economy does not keep the same composition over time. The relative importance of services, manufacturing, digital activity, household consumption and different forms of investment changes. If old weights remain in use for too long, estimates may describe yesterday’s economy less accurately. A newer base can incorporate recent data sources, updated classifications and improved methods. It can also revise historical estimates, altering the reported pace of growth without changing the actual sequence of events.

A new series therefore requires a bridge between old and new estimates. Analysts need to know which differences arise from updated source data, which follow from altered classifications and which result from a changed conceptual treatment. Without that explanation, a reader may conclude that an administration has created growth or erased it simply by changing the base year. A revision can be methodologically justified and still require transparent communication because public debate often treats a headline growth rate as a political scorecard.

The new series should not be evaluated solely by whether a particular quarter’s growth rate is higher or lower. A sound review asks whether the accounts cover relevant activities more completely, whether the methods are internationally intelligible and whether data allow meaningful comparison over time. It also asks whether limitations are disclosed. No national account can capture every aspect of welfare: unpaid care, environmental depletion and income distribution require other indicators.

National accounts remain essential for assessing output and production. Their usefulness increases when readers understand what they measure and what they do not. The base-year update is both a technical revision and a communication task. The public needs a stable explanation of the method, not an assumption that every revision is either a discovery of hidden prosperity or evidence of statistical manipulation.

sources.title: Press Note on New Series of GDP Estimates with Base Year 2022-23
sources.publisher: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Government of India

passages.title: The Belém package connects climate pledges with implementation
passages.text:
The Belém Political Package emerged from the thirtieth Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, held in Brazil in 2025. The package consists of decisions adopted through the conference process and covers issues often debated separately: climate finance, international cooperation, nationally determined contributions, transparency and the gap between stated ambition and implementation. The documents matter not because they create one universal climate code, but because they record negotiated decisions under the existing climate framework.

One difficulty in climate diplomacy is the distance between a national pledge and the measures required to meet it. A country may announce a target, but delivery depends on domestic legislation, investment, technology, institutional capacity and public reporting. The UNFCCC process includes mechanisms for communicating and reviewing national contributions and reporting progress. Transparency can help parties and the public understand what has been done, but it does not by itself build a transmission line, protect a coastal settlement or finance an adaptation project.

Finance remains a recurring point of tension. Developing countries argue that climate action requires resources as well as policy ambition, particularly where they face high exposure to climate impacts and have limited fiscal space. Negotiations involve predictability, access, public and private sources, concessional terms and the capacity to prepare viable projects. A fund that exists on paper may be difficult to use if its application process is opaque or technical requirements exceed a local authority’s capacity.

The Belém decisions also addressed concerns about trade-related measures taken in the name of climate policy. Governments may pursue environmental objectives through standards or border measures, but other States may question whether such measures are discriminatory or disproportionately restrictive. The package places these concerns within the wider discussion of cooperation rather than treating them as unrelated to climate action.

A conference decision cannot guarantee that every State will implement the same policy or achieve its target. Its contribution is more practical: it clarifies negotiated expectations, provides a forum for review and identifies areas where cooperation is needed. The value of the package will depend on whether governments convert agreed language into budgets, rules, projects and verifiable results.

sources.title: Belém Political Package
sources.publisher: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

passages.title: The digital rupee is a claim on the central bank
passages.text:
The Reserve Bank of India’s Digital Rupee (e₹) often appears in public discussion beside mobile payment applications, but the concepts are not identical. A payment interface can move money held in a bank account, while a central-bank digital currency is itself a digital form of central-bank money. The RBI describes e₹ as the digital form of the physical rupee, issued by the central bank and held in a digital wallet. It is intended to offer features associated with cash, including convenience and finality of settlement.

The RBI’s frequently asked questions, updated on 1 October 2026, state that the digital rupee is being piloted in retail and wholesale segments. Retail use concerns members of the public and merchants; wholesale use concerns banks and other institutions. Wallets are offered by participating banks and non-banks. The existence of a wallet does not turn every payment made through an ordinary application into a digital-rupee transaction. The underlying instrument matters, not merely the appearance of a payment screen.

A central-bank liability differs from a commercial-bank deposit. A deposit is a claim against the bank that holds the account, subject to the banking framework. The digital rupee, by contrast, represents central-bank money in digital form. This distinction may matter for settlement, monetary infrastructure and the design of future payment systems. It does not mean every user must abandon bank accounts or that physical currency will immediately disappear.

The pilot raises design questions familiar to any public payment system. Users need accessible wallets, clear instructions and reliable grievance channels. Merchants must understand how to accept the instrument, and participating institutions must manage security and operational risks. A digital wallet can improve convenience while still creating barriers for people who lack a compatible device or are uncomfortable with digital interfaces. The presence of a digital option should not be mistaken for universal access.

The RBI’s FAQs describe the instrument and the pilot; they do not announce a completed nationwide replacement of cash. The policy significance lies in testing how central-bank money can operate in a digital environment. Adoption, interoperability, privacy, resilience and user trust will influence whether the experiment becomes a lasting part of the payments landscape. e₹ is a developing monetary instrument, not simply another brand of instant payment application.

sources.publisher: Reserve Bank of India

passages.title: A hearing before a public permit is withdrawn
passages.text:
Assume a municipal licensing code contains this rule. A public authority may suspend a trading permit immediately where credible evidence shows an imminent and serious risk to public safety. In all other cases, it must give the permit-holder notice of the material allegations, a reasonable opportunity to respond and a decision explaining the evidence relied upon. A hearing need not be oral if the written process allows the person to address the decisive facts. The authority may protect confidential sources, but it must disclose a fair summary of the allegation.

The rule recognises that public safety sometimes requires action before a full inquiry can be completed. That exception is narrow. A general concern, an unverified complaint or administrative pressure does not by itself establish an imminent and serious risk. Where an immediate suspension is justified, the authority must provide a prompt post-suspension review. The review must be conducted by an officer who did not make the initial emergency decision.

The permit-holder’s opportunity to respond must be meaningful rather than ceremonial. A notice that says only “public complaints have been received” does not identify what conduct is questioned. A notice specifying the date, location and alleged obstruction may allow a useful written response even if the authority does not disclose the complainant’s name. The authority need not reveal information whose disclosure would create a genuine risk to a witness, but it cannot rely on a secret allegation without explaining its substance.

A decision-maker must consider relevant replies. It need not accept every explanation, and it may find that a reply is unsupported. But a decision that simply repeats the original complaint without addressing a material response does not demonstrate that the opportunity to be heard was real. The written reasons need not resemble a court judgment; they must identify the decisive facts and explain why the permit is suspended or restored.

Apply only this hypothetical rule. Do not assume an automatic right to an oral hearing, that every suspension is invalid, or that the authority must disclose a confidential witness’s identity. The decisive questions are the seriousness and immediacy of the risk, the adequacy of the disclosed allegation, and the quality of the review and reasons. The requirement can be tested by asking whether the person could identify the conduct to be answered, whether the authority considered the response, and whether the reasons connect the evidence to the chosen measure. A brief order may be sufficient when the facts are simple, but brevity cannot substitute for explaining a disputed decisive point.

passages.title: A photograph and the chain of custody
passages.text:
Assume a fictional evidence rule for a public inquiry. A digital photograph may be considered if the party relying on it can show that it fairly represents the scene at the relevant time and can explain how the file was obtained and preserved. The rule does not require a professional photographer. It does require enough information to assess whether the image has been altered, misdated or separated from its original context. Metadata may assist, but metadata alone is not conclusive.

A party offering the image must identify the device or account from which it was obtained, the person who transferred it and any editing or conversion performed before submission. If an image has been cropped to protect a bystander’s identity, the original must be preserved and the change disclosed. A crop does not automatically make an image inadmissible; concealment of a material feature may affect the weight given to it.

The inquiry may consider an image even where the chain is incomplete, but it must distinguish admissibility from reliability. A minor gap that has no bearing on the relevant feature may reduce weight only slightly. A gap that makes it impossible to determine whether the time stamp was changed or whether the image depicts the correct location may be decisive. The party opposing the image may test the account of the transfer and propose an alternative explanation.

Suppose a shopkeeper submits a photograph showing a damaged shutter. The file was sent through a messaging service that compresses images. The shopkeeper retains the original on the phone and explains that a date stamp was added by the camera application. The other side may ask for the original file and challenge whether the date setting was accurate. Compression alone does not prove tampering, and a camera-generated date is evidence of a setting, not necessarily proof of the actual time.

The rule aims to make digital evidence usable without treating every file as self-authenticating. The inquiry must ask whether the image is connected to the event, whether changes are disclosed and whether the opposing party has a fair opportunity to test its reliability. Apply only this fictional rule; do not assume every digital image requires an expert certificate. For example, a transfer log showing the original file’s creation, the date it was copied and the identity of the person who submitted it may fill a gap that would otherwise invite doubt. A witness who can explain the handling of the file may also be relevant, although the rule does not make such testimony an automatic condition for every image.

passages.title: A contract that delegates only a limited task
passages.text:
Assume a commercial agency rule. A principal authorises an agent to negotiate supply contracts up to a stated price and quantity. The agent may make routine decisions within those limits, but may not change the delivery location, grant exclusive distribution rights or waive a quality requirement unless the principal separately agrees. A supplier who knows the limits cannot rely on the agent’s apparent authority to make a prohibited change. A supplier who has received no notice of the limits may rely on a reasonable representation of authority made by the principal, provided the supplier does not ignore facts that call for inquiry.

The rule separates internal permission from representations made to outsiders. A principal may give an agent broad-looking authority in a meeting or email and then privately impose narrower instructions. If the principal’s own conduct reasonably leads a supplier to believe that the agent can act, the principal may be bound within the scope of that representation. But the agent cannot create apparent authority merely by asserting that it exists. The representation must be traceable to the principal.

A supplier’s knowledge matters. If a contract document clearly states that the agent cannot grant exclusivity, the supplier cannot later say that it believed the agent had that power. Likewise, a supplier who sees a price plainly outside the stated range may be expected to ask for confirmation. The rule does not require outsiders to investigate every routine instruction; it does require them to respond to obvious warning signs.

A later ratification can change the result. If the principal, knowing the material facts, expressly adopts the agent’s unauthorised change, the principal becomes bound by that change under this hypothetical rule. Mere silence does not amount to ratification unless the principal’s conduct clearly communicates adoption. Accepting a benefit while knowing the relevant terms may be evidence of such conduct, but the facts must be assessed carefully.

Apply the rule to the authority granted and the supplier’s knowledge. Do not assume that every act by an agent binds a principal, or that private restrictions always protect the principal against an outsider who reasonably relied on the principal’s own representation. A supplier should therefore read the authority documents as a whole. A principal’s public description of the agent’s role may be relevant, but a later document delivered to the supplier can narrow what reliance remains reasonable. The timing and clarity of each communication matter when deciding what the supplier knew at the moment of agreement.

passages.title: A public path across privately owned land
passages.text:
Assume a fictional land-use principle. A landowner may exclude the public from private land unless the land has been dedicated as a public path or a statutory access right applies. Dedication requires clear conduct showing an intention to permit public passage as a lasting right, rather than occasional tolerance. The public authority must establish the route’s location and the owner’s conduct. Long use by itself is relevant but not conclusive.

An owner may allow neighbours to cross a field for years as a matter of courtesy. If the owner regularly closes the gate for private events, tells users that the permission may be withdrawn and maintains a sign describing the crossing as a temporary favour, the conduct may indicate permission rather than dedication. By contrast, a landowner who lays a permanent path, invites the public to use it and enters it on a publicly distributed access map may have shown an intention beyond neighbourly tolerance.

The principle also protects reasonable reliance. If residents have been openly invited to use a path and have organised access to a school or clinic around it, a sudden closure may create serious hardship. That reliance does not itself create a public right where dedication is absent. It may, however, support a request for a negotiated easement, a temporary access order under another rule or compensation for a public acquisition. The inquiry must not confuse a fair policy outcome with the legal test for dedication.

A dispute about the route requires accurate evidence. A map may show the line drawn by an authority, but the actual path on the ground may have shifted when a stream changed course. Witness statements, maintenance records, photographs and the owner’s communications can help establish whether users followed the same route and whether the owner treated it as public. An authority cannot use a broad map label to bypass the requirement to prove the route.

Under this hypothetical principle, the decisive question is intention demonstrated by conduct, considered with evidence of use. The number of people who crossed the land matters, but it does not replace proof that the owner meant to create a lasting public right. The rule therefore balances private control, public access and reliable evidence. If the owner maintained a gate but supplied keys to every household and described the route as a permanent community access, those facts may point in a different direction from a sign reserving a revocable favour. Neither a key nor a sign decides the dispute alone; the authority must evaluate the pattern of conduct and the route evidence together.

passages.title: A public claim made by a private platform
passages.text:
Assume a consumer-information rule applying to online platforms. A platform that republishes a seller’s factual claim must take reasonable steps to avoid presenting a materially misleading claim as verified information. The platform is not automatically responsible for every statement uploaded by a user. Its responsibility increases where it edits the claim, adds its own verification mark, earns a fee specifically for promoting the claim or receives a credible notice identifying a factual error and continues to promote it without review.

The rule distinguishes neutral hosting from active endorsement. A platform may display a seller’s description with a clear label that it is supplied by the seller. It may also remove or restrict a claim under a transparent moderation policy. But if the platform adds a badge reading “independently tested” without having conducted or reviewed any test, it has made a representation of its own. The seller’s original claim and the platform’s added endorsement must be assessed separately.

Notice is relevant but not conclusive. A competitor’s bare assertion that a product claim is false does not require immediate removal. A detailed laboratory report, a regulator’s alert or a correction from the product’s manufacturer may provide a credible basis for review. The platform must consider the reliability and relevance of the notice. It need not accept every complaint, but it cannot treat a specific and well-supported warning as though it were merely an opinion.

A platform that earns a fee for placement is not automatically prohibited from carrying the advertisement. It must make the commercial relationship clear and must not imply that paid visibility is an independent quality assessment. A disclaimer buried in an unrelated page may be insufficient if the main display gives consumers a contrary impression. The overall presentation matters, including the badge, ranking label and language surrounding the claim.

Apply only this fictional rule. It does not impose strict liability for every user post and does not guarantee that all online information is accurate. It asks whether the platform’s own conduct, commercial incentives or response to credible notice created or maintained a misleading impression that reasonable care could have prevented. A platform that receives a substantiated warning should also record how it assessed the material and why it chose to retain, qualify or remove the claim. That record may help demonstrate reasonable care, but a paper trail cannot cure a decision that ignored a clear factual contradiction.

passages.title: A promise to reduce avoidable loss
passages.text:
Assume a fictional contract rule on compensation. A party that suffers a breach may claim losses caused by the breach and reasonably foreseeable when the contract was made. The claimant must take reasonable steps to limit avoidable loss, but is not required to take an extraordinary risk or incur disproportionate expense. If the claimant unreasonably refuses a practical substitute, compensation may be reduced by the loss that could reasonably have been avoided.

The rule distinguishes an ordinary response from an unrealistic demand. A buyer whose supplier fails to deliver a standard component may be expected to seek an available replacement at a modest additional cost. The buyer is not required to purchase a substitute that is technically incompatible or that would expose the business to a serious safety risk. A seller cannot insist that a buyer spend more than the value of the contract simply to demonstrate that every alternative was explored.

The claimant must also keep records that allow the loss to be assessed. Invoices, replacement quotations, delivery notices and internal communications may show what alternatives were available and when. The rule does not demand perfect paperwork, but a claimant who gives no explanation for a large increase in claimed costs may struggle to establish that the increase was caused by the breach rather than by an independent business decision.

Causation remains important. If a factory shuts down because a power failure unrelated to the supplier’s delay occurs on the same day, the buyer cannot attribute all lost production to the supplier. If the delay made the factory vulnerable to the power interruption, the analysis may be more complex, but the claimant must still connect the claimed loss to the breach. Foreseeability is assessed from information reasonably available when the parties contracted, not from hindsight.

The rule seeks compensation rather than punishment. It places the claimant in the position that would probably have existed if the contract had been performed, subject to causation, foreseeability and reasonable mitigation. Apply only the stated rule; do not assume a party must accept every substitute or that any failure to mitigate eliminates the entire claim. The claimant should explain why an alternative was not reasonably usable. A replacement may be available in the market yet unsuitable because it does not meet a technical specification, cannot arrive within a relevant period or would expose workers to a foreseeable hazard. The evaluation concerns practical alternatives at the time, not options identified with hindsight.

passages.title: A relocation plan needs a counterfactual
passages.text:
A district authority proposes relocating households from a riverbank settlement before the next monsoon. Its report records repeated flooding, damage to electrical connections and the cost of emergency repairs. It concludes that relocation will reduce public expenditure and improve safety. The report is persuasive about exposure in the existing settlement, but gives little information about the alternatives offered to residents or the cost of maintaining the new site.

A relocation programme should be assessed against a realistic counterfactual: what would happen if the settlement remained, with feasible protective measures? Raising electrical fittings, restoring a drainage channel and creating an evacuation route may reduce some risks, although they will not remove every danger. The authority must compare those measures with the full cost of relocation, including transport, employment access, school continuity and the risk that households will return if the new site is distant from livelihoods.

The report treats the value of land released for public use as a saving. That is not necessarily wrong, but it is not the same as a saving in the public budget. If the land is later used for a commercial project, the authority should disclose whether that use is part of the relocation rationale. Otherwise, the public may be asked to accept a safety justification while the decision is partly driven by land value. The two reasons can coexist, but they should not be conflated.

The authority’s strongest argument is that repeated flooding creates a risk that cannot be managed indefinitely through emergency repairs. Its weakest inference is that a new site will automatically be safer. A site with poor transport, inadequate water supply or uncertain tenure can create different forms of insecurity. The authority should publish a site assessment and explain how affected households will participate in deciding whether the offered location is workable.

The report also needs to distinguish the number of homes moved from the number of households that can remain safely at the new location. A family may accept a plot but lose access to work, school or a shared care network. Such a household might later return to the riverbank, turning a one-time construction cost into repeated expenditure. Conversely, if the new site is connected to transport and services, the move may produce a benefit that cannot be achieved through a raised road or an evacuation plan alone.

A sound decision does not require that every resident agree. It requires reasons complete enough to compare options and a way to test the predicted benefit after relocation. Without a counterfactual, the authority can show that the current situation is costly but not that its chosen alternative is better.

passages.title: A city index hides the distribution
passages.text:
The mayor announces that a new “liveability score” has risen by twelve points. The index combines average commute time, public-space area, air quality and access to basic services. The mayor argues that the improvement demonstrates that the city is becoming more liveable and that the current development strategy should continue. The score is useful as a summary, but the conclusion is broader than the evidence presented.

An average can rise even when some neighbourhoods become worse. A new park may improve the city-wide public-space measure while residents in a distant settlement lose access to a bus route. A fall in average commute time may reflect faster travel for office workers while informal workers face longer journeys because of a route change. The index does not necessarily conceal these outcomes intentionally; it simply cannot display every distributional effect in one number.

The index also combines measures that can move in different directions. If air quality improves while access to services declines, the final score depends on the weight assigned to each component. A change in weighting may alter the headline even if no neighbourhood experiences a different physical condition. The city should publish the components and explain how weights were selected. A score without its construction method is not an adequate basis for comparing policies.

The mayor’s strongest point is that a composite measure can help residents follow progress across multiple objectives. The strongest objection is not that indexes are useless, but that a single figure should not substitute for a distributional account. The city can retain the index while publishing neighbourhood-level data, disaggregated travel times and a description of who gained or lost access to a service.

A further question concerns the choice of weights. Assigning the same numerical weight to air quality and commute time is not a purely technical act; it reflects a view about the relative importance of those outcomes. A city could consult residents, publish sensitivity tests showing how alternative weights change the result and explain whether the score is intended to track minimum living conditions or general improvement. Without such disclosures, a precise-looking number may hide a contestable value judgment.

The development strategy may still be defensible. The index alone does not prove it. A city should evaluate whether changes are shared, whether the weights reflect public priorities and whether groups with the poorest starting position are improving. A better score is evidence of movement in the chosen measures; it is not a complete moral or policy verdict.

passages.title: The railway station is not the whole journey
passages.text:
A transport agency evaluates a new suburban rail service by counting passengers entering and leaving the station. The first quarter shows a substantial increase in boardings, so the agency concludes that the service has improved access to employment. The measure captures use of the rail line, but it does not show whether passengers can reach the station conveniently or whether destinations served are places where jobs are available.

A commuter’s journey begins before the platform. A person may walk along an unlit road, wait for an infrequent feeder bus or pay for a motorcycle ride. Another may live close to the station but work in an industrial area that requires two transfers. If a passenger boards the train but leaves the network before reaching the job centre, the boarding count records demand without demonstrating access. The agency should therefore examine door-to-door time, transfer reliability and the geographic match between stations and employment.

The agency responds that passenger counts are objective and inexpensive. They allow comparison across time and can identify stations where demand is growing. The problem arises only when a narrow measure is used to support a broader conclusion. A rise in boardings may reflect population growth, a fare discount, a change in ticket counting or a temporary event. It may also reflect genuine improved access. The count alone cannot distinguish these explanations.

A practical evaluation would combine counts with household travel surveys, feeder-service data, employment locations and observations of transfer delays. The sample need not be perfect to improve analysis, but limitations should be disclosed. The agency should also examine who is not using the service. Low use may reflect a lack of demand, but it may also reflect inaccessible stations, unsafe walking routes or fares high relative to income.

The agency should test its data at different times of day. A station may be busy during the morning peak but offer poor connections for shift workers travelling at night. A single monthly average can conceal the absence of late services or long waits on Sundays. Household travel diaries can reveal these gaps, while origin-destination data can show whether a rail journey actually connects people with employment clusters rather than merely moving them between residential areas.

The rail service may have succeeded at attracting passengers. Whether it has improved access to employment is a separate proposition requiring further evidence. Transport investment should be judged by the journeys it makes possible, not merely by activity at the station gate.

passages.title: A laboratory’s result needs a comparison group
passages.text:
A district health department introduces a text-message reminder system for patients who have missed routine vaccination appointments. After three months, clinics using reminders report a higher attendance rate than they did in the previous quarter. The department concludes that the messages caused the improvement and proposes extending them to every clinic. The result is encouraging, but the comparison does not isolate the effect of the messages.

Attendance may have changed for other reasons. The district may have opened a new bus route, expanded clinic hours or carried out a public awareness campaign at the same time. Seasonal illness may have altered how often families visited health facilities. The clinics selected for the pilot may also have had better staff or more accurate contact details than clinics not included. Any of these factors could affect attendance independently of reminders.

A stronger evaluation would compare clinics that introduce reminders with similar clinics that do not, while checking whether the groups had comparable attendance trends before the pilot. If random assignment is practical and ethical, it can reduce the risk that pilot clinics are systematically different. If not, the department can match clinics on relevant features and measure changes over the same period. The evaluation should record undelivered messages and households without reliable phone access, since a reminder system may reach some groups more easily than others.

The department’s argument also treats attendance as the final objective. Yet a reminder may increase visits without ensuring that a vaccine is available, that a clinician is present or that the family receives the correct dose. A system should measure completed vaccination, not merely arrival at the clinic. It should also protect contact information and explain how families can opt out.

The design should be assessed for unintended effects. A reminder sent to a shared family phone could disclose sensitive information; a message delivered in a language a caregiver does not read may create little benefit. A helpline may be needed for families who change numbers or wish to correct an appointment. These details do not decide whether reminders work, but they affect whether the service is fair, trusted and usable.

These limitations do not show that reminders are ineffective. They show that the observed rise is not enough to establish their effect or equity. A promising intervention deserves a better test before it is scaled. The department should preserve useful operational data, compare outcomes carefully and keep the service accessible to families who do not rely on text messages.

passages.title: A district's flood-resilience budget
passages.text: A district allocates ₹48 crore to flood-resilience work. Of this amount, 35% is reserved for drainage rehabilitation, 25% for wetland restoration, 20% for raised electrical infrastructure and the balance for community warning systems. During the first quarter, 60% of the drainage allocation and 50% of the wetland allocation are spent. The electrical programme spends ₹6 crore. Treat all figures as exact and assume no funds are transferred between heads. No transfers are assumed between the four budget heads.

passages.title: A mobile health outreach schedule
passages.text: A mobile clinic operates for three full days and one final half-day. It serves 48 patients on each full day and 30 patients during the half-day. On the first full day, villages A and B are each assigned 25% of that day’s capacity. On the second full day, village C is assigned 20% of capacity; the remaining places on that day are divided equally between villages D and E. The third full day is reserved for follow-up referrals from all five villages. The final half-day is used only for follow-up visits. Use the stated capacity, not the number of staff.

passages.title: A port's container inspection data
passages.text: A port inspected 1,200 containers in a week. 45% were selected for documentary checks, 30% for physical checks and the rest received both checks. Of the documentary-only group, 80% were cleared on the same day. Of the physical-only group, 65% were cleared on the same day. The combined-check group contained 120 containers cleared on the same day. Assume the three groups are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. The weekly total includes every container in only one of these three categories.

That fragile paper requires preservation.

options.text: Authenticated diagnostic access for trained technicians.

the use of a measuring instrument to test battery voltage.

The opinion has no legal authority and must be ignored.

The opportunity to respond may have been merely ceremonial because a material reply was not considered.
A written process is always invalid without an oral hearing.
The permit-holder was entitled to select the deciding officer.

questions.explanation: The rule requires relevant replies to be considered and reasons to identify decisive facts.

questions.prompt: After an emergency suspension, who should conduct the prompt review? (Passage: “A hearing before a public permit is withdrawn”)

options.text: The complainant acting as the licensing authority.
The same officer without reviewing new material.
An officer who did not make the initial emergency decision.
Any person selected by the permit-holder.

questions.explanation: The rule expressly requires an independent officer for the post-suspension review.

questions.prompt: What must the party relying on the photograph establish? (Passage: “A photograph and the chain of custody”)

options.text: That every metadata field is necessarily accurate.
That a professional photographer took the image.
That the file was never compressed by any application.
That it fairly represents the scene and that its acquisition and preservation can be explained.

questions.explanation: The rule focuses on fair representation and an explainable chain, not professional authorship.

questions.prompt: The shopkeeper retains the original but sent a compressed copy through a messaging service. What follows? (Passage: “A photograph and the chain of custody”)

options.text: Compression alone does not prove tampering; the original and transfer history can be examined.
The photograph must be excluded automatically.
The compressed copy conclusively proves the event time.
The opposing party loses the right to challenge the photograph.

questions.explanation: The rule distinguishes ordinary processing from concealed material alteration.

questions.prompt: Why does the passage distinguish admissibility from reliability? (Passage: “A photograph and the chain of custody”)

options.text: Every admissible image must be treated as conclusive proof.
An image may be considered while still receiving reduced weight because of gaps in its history.
A reliable image can never be challenged by another party.
The two concepts are interchangeable under the rule.

questions.explanation: The inquiry may consider an image while separately assessing its evidentiary weight.

questions.prompt: A party crops out a bystander, preserves the original and discloses the edit. Which statement is best? (Passage: “A photograph and the chain of custody”)

options.text: The original may be destroyed once the cropped image is filed.
Any cropping makes the image inadmissible.
The crop is not automatically disqualifying, though concealment of a material feature may affect weight.
The edit need not be disclosed if made for privacy.

questions.explanation: The rule permits a disclosed crop if the original is preserved, subject to its effect on context.

questions.prompt: Which question is most relevant when the date stamp is disputed? (Passage: “A photograph and the chain of custody”)

options.text: Whether the messaging service has a large user base.
Whether the shopkeeper owns the building.
Whether the image was taken in colour.
Whether the camera’s date setting accurately reflected the time of capture.

questions.explanation: A device date is evidence of a setting, not conclusive proof of actual time.

questions.prompt: Which source can create apparent authority under the rule? (Passage: “A contract that delegates only a limited task”)

options.text: A reasonable representation of authority made by the principal.
An agent’s unsupported statement about their own powers.
A supplier’s private assumption about what is convenient.
A contract clause written after the transaction.

questions.explanation: The representation must be traceable to the principal.

questions.prompt: The supplier receives a document expressly prohibiting the agent from granting exclusivity. The agent nevertheless grants it. What follows? (Passage: “A contract that delegates only a limited task”)

options.text: The principal is bound because every agent has unlimited authority.
The supplier cannot rely on apparent authority because it knew the relevant limit.
The supplier may ignore the restriction if the price is fair.
The agent’s statement overrides the written instruction.

questions.explanation: A supplier who knows the limit cannot rely on apparent authority for the prohibited change.

questions.prompt: The principal knows the agent changed the delivery location without permission and later expressly adopts the change. What is the effect? (Passage: “A contract that delegates only a limited task”)

options.text: The supplier becomes the agent’s principal.
The change remains void because authority can never be ratified.
The principal is bound by the unauthorised change through ratification.
The principal is bound only if the supplier makes a new offer.

questions.explanation: The rule allows knowing and express adoption to ratify the agent’s act.

questions.prompt: Why must an apparent-authority representation come from the principal? (Passage: “A contract that delegates only a limited task”)

options.text: A supplier is required to know every private instruction.
An agent is never permitted to negotiate a contract.
A principal cannot communicate with suppliers.
An agent cannot enlarge their own power merely by claiming to possess it.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes the principal’s outward representation from the agent’s self-assertion.

questions.prompt: Which circumstance is most likely to require a supplier to make further inquiry? (Passage: “A contract that delegates only a limited task”)

options.text: A proposed price plainly exceeds the range stated in the documents received by the supplier.
The agent signs a routine order within the stated quantity and price.
The supplier receives a standard invoice after delivery.
The principal has previously paid invoices on time.

questions.explanation: An obvious departure from stated limits is a warning sign under the rule.

questions.prompt: What is necessary to establish dedication of a public path? (Passage: “A public path across privately owned land”)

options.text: Any use by neighbours for a long period.
Clear conduct showing an intention to permit lasting public passage.
A map label drawn by the public authority alone.
The absence of a fence around the land.

questions.explanation: The rule requires intention to create a lasting right; use is relevant but not conclusive.

questions.prompt: An owner permits neighbours to cross but repeatedly says the permission may be withdrawn. What does this suggest? (Passage: “A public path across privately owned land”)

options.text: The authority may acquire the land without further evidence.
The path is automatically dedicated after one year.
The crossing may be tolerated by permission rather than dedicated as a public right.
The owner has abandoned all rights over the field.

questions.explanation: The owner's reservation is evidence against an intention to dedicate.

questions.prompt: Residents relied on an invited path to reach a clinic. Does that reliance alone establish dedication? (Passage: “A public path across privately owned land”)

options.text: No; reliance is irrelevant for every purpose.
Yes; reliance automatically converts permission into a public right.
Yes; any hardship eliminates the need to prove the owner’s intention.
No; it may support other remedies or negotiation but does not replace the dedication test.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes reliance-based concerns from the legal test for dedication.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most directly help establish the owner’s intention? (Passage: “A public path across privately owned land”)

options.text: The owner’s invitations, access maps and maintenance of a permanent public route.
A general map showing the nearest town centre.
The number of vehicles parked on an unrelated road.
A resident’s estimate of the property’s market value.

questions.explanation: The principle focuses on conduct indicating whether passage was intended to be lasting.

questions.prompt: Why is the actual route’s location important? (Passage: “A public path across privately owned land”)

options.text: The legal test depends only on the number of users.
A public authority must prove the route rather than rely solely on a broad map label.
A path may move whenever an owner changes a gate.
A map is conclusive even if the physical route has shifted.

questions.explanation: The authority must establish the route’s location with supporting evidence.

questions.prompt: When does the platform’s responsibility increase under the rule? (Passage: “A public claim made by a private platform”)

options.text: Only when the seller has no commercial relationship with the platform.
Whenever any user uploads any statement.
When it endorses, edits, specifically promotes or ignores a credible notice about a material error.
Whenever a consumer disagrees with a product’s price.

questions.explanation: The first paragraph identifies the platform actions that increase responsibility.

questions.prompt: A platform adds an “independently tested” badge without reviewing any test. What is the strongest analysis? (Passage: “A public claim made by a private platform”)

options.text: The platform may rely on the seller’s statement without further inquiry.
The badge is irrelevant because the seller uploaded the original description.
The platform is automatically liable for every product defect.
The badge is the platform’s own representation and must be assessed separately from the seller’s claim.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes neutral hosting from an added endorsement made by the platform.

questions.prompt: A competitor sends only an unsupported message saying a claim is false. What does the rule require? (Passage: “A public claim made by a private platform”)

options.text: The platform need not treat the bare assertion as credible notice requiring immediate removal.
The platform must remove the claim immediately.
The platform must accept every competitor’s statement as evidence.
The platform must suspend the seller permanently.

questions.explanation: The rule distinguishes an unsupported assertion from a specific, reliable warning.

questions.prompt: Why must paid placement be clearly disclosed? (Passage: “A public claim made by a private platform”)

options.text: Paid promotion is prohibited in every circumstance.
Consumers should not mistake commercial visibility for an independent quality assessment.
The platform’s ranking system must be operated by the seller.
A disclaimer can never affect the overall impression.

questions.explanation: A fee may be permitted but the commercial relationship must not be misrepresented.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most strongly support a duty to review a product claim? (Passage: “A public claim made by a private platform”)

options.text: A competitor’s anonymous statement with no supporting material.
An unrelated customer complaint about delivery packaging.
A regulator’s alert identifying the specific factual error in the promoted claim.
A social media poll about the product’s popularity.

questions.explanation: A regulator alert is a concrete example of a credible basis for review.

questions.prompt: What does the mitigation requirement demand? (Passage: “A promise to reduce avoidable loss”)

options.text: A complete waiver of compensation after any delay.
Acceptance of every available substitute regardless of safety.
An obligation to spend any amount necessary to avoid loss.
Reasonable steps to limit avoidable loss without extraordinary risk or disproportionate expense.

questions.explanation: The rule requires reasonable action, not an unlimited duty to avoid all loss.

questions.prompt: A buyer rejects a modestly priced, technically compatible replacement and suffers additional avoidable loss. What may follow? (Passage: “A promise to reduce avoidable loss”)

options.text: Compensation may be reduced by the loss that could reasonably have been avoided.
The buyer automatically loses every claim arising from the breach.
The supplier must pay all costs without regard to the substitute.
The buyer is required to accept a dangerous replacement.

questions.explanation: The rule permits reduction where a practical substitute was unreasonably refused.

questions.prompt: Why does the rule require the claimant to retain quotations and delivery records? (Passage: “A promise to reduce avoidable loss”)

options.text: They prove that the contract was written.
They help establish which alternatives were available and whether claimed costs were caused by the breach.
They determine whether the claimant intended to make a profit.
They replace the need to establish foreseeability.

questions.explanation: Records help assess mitigation, timing and causation.

questions.prompt: A factory also loses production because of an unrelated power failure. What must the claimant establish? (Passage: “A promise to reduce avoidable loss”)

options.text: That every loss occurring after a breach is recoverable.
That the supplier controlled the electricity grid.
A causal connection between the supplier’s breach and the loss claimed.
That foreseeability is assessed only after the breach.

questions.explanation: The rule excludes losses arising independently of the breach unless the required connection is shown.

questions.prompt: What is the rule’s overall remedial purpose? (Passage: “A promise to reduce avoidable loss”)

options.text: To eliminate the need for evidence of loss.
To punish a party whenever a contract is broken.
To guarantee the claimant the most profitable outcome possible.
To compensate for foreseeable loss caused by breach, subject to reasonable mitigation.

questions.explanation: The passage describes compensation rather than punishment.

questions.prompt: Which assumption is most important to the authority’s conclusion that relocation will improve safety? (Passage: “A relocation plan needs a counterfactual”)

options.text: The offered site will expose residents to lower overall risk than the existing settlement and feasible upgrades.
The current settlement has never experienced flooding.
Emergency repairs will become free after relocation.
All residents work within walking distance of the riverbank.

questions.explanation: The authority compares existing risk with a destination that has not been adequately assessed.

questions.prompt: Which additional evidence would most strengthen the authority’s case? (Passage: “A relocation plan needs a counterfactual”)

options.text: The number of photographs taken during the last flood.
A comparative assessment of flood risk, services, tenure and livelihood access at the proposed site.
The market value of unrelated buildings in the district.
A survey asking whether residents like the authority’s logo.

questions.explanation: The missing premise concerns whether the destination is actually safer and workable.

questions.prompt: Which fact would most weaken the claim that relocation reduces public expenditure? (Passage: “A relocation plan needs a counterfactual”)

options.text: Emergency electrical repairs have been costly.
The current settlement experienced three floods in five years.
The new site requires expensive transport services and recurring infrastructure maintenance.
The authority recorded the number of damaged connections.

questions.explanation: High recurring costs at the destination undermine the claimed expenditure saving.

questions.prompt: Why is the land-value argument treated separately from safety? (Passage: “A relocation plan needs a counterfactual”)

options.text: Safety and commercial considerations cannot coexist in one decision.
A public authority may never consider the value of land.
Land values are always unrelated to public expenditure.
A possible commercial benefit does not establish that relocation is the safest or fairest option.

questions.explanation: The passage says the motives may coexist but should not be conflated.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows from the passage? (Passage: “A relocation plan needs a counterfactual”)

options.text: The current settlement’s danger does not by itself prove that the proposed site is preferable.
Any relocation plan should be rejected if one resident objects.
Emergency repairs are always cheaper than planned relocation.
A counterfactual is unnecessary when a report contains flood photographs.

questions.explanation: The author distinguishes evidence of an existing problem from evidence that a solution is better.

questions.prompt: Which change would most directly address the report’s central weakness? (Passage: “A relocation plan needs a counterfactual”)

options.text: Remove the section describing emergency repair costs.
Publish a comparison of realistic protection-in-place options and the full consequences of the proposed move.
Use the released land’s market price as the sole success measure.
Stop recording the experiences of affected households.

questions.explanation: The report needs a proper comparison of alternatives and the costs households bear.

questions.prompt: Which assumption underlies the mayor’s argument? (Passage: “A city index hides the distribution”)

options.text: The index excludes air quality and public-space measures.
Every neighbourhood experienced the same improvement.
The composite score captures enough of residents’ experiences to justify continuing the same strategy.
The weights never affect the final score.

questions.explanation: The mayor moves from an aggregate change to a broad claim about city-wide liveability.

questions.prompt: Which example best illustrates the passage’s concern about averages? (Passage: “A city index hides the distribution”)

options.text: The city publishes the weights used in the index.
Every neighbourhood receives the same bus frequency.
Air quality and public-space area both improve equally.
Office workers’ journeys become faster while informal workers’ journeys lengthen.

questions.explanation: Aggregate improvement can coexist with unequal outcomes across groups.

questions.prompt: Which disclosure would most strengthen the usefulness of the index? (Passage: “A city index hides the distribution”)

options.text: Component scores, weighting methods and neighbourhood-level outcomes.
Only the final headline score and a mayoral speech.
A list of new buildings without travel or service data.
The date on which the index was first proposed.

questions.explanation: The passage asks for transparency about construction and distributional effects.

questions.prompt: Which statement would weaken the claim that the twelve-point rise reflects physical improvement? (Passage: “A city index hides the distribution”)

options.text: A new park opened in a previously underserved district.
The score rose chiefly because the city changed the weights while measured neighbourhood conditions remained unchanged.
Air quality improved across several neighbourhoods.
The city reduced average commute time for most groups.

questions.explanation: A weighting change without physical change undermines the interpretation of the score as improved conditions.

questions.prompt: What is the author’s view of composite indexes? (Passage: “A city index hides the distribution”)

options.text: They are sufficient to determine all public priorities.
They are always misleading and should be discontinued.
They can summarise progress but should be accompanied by disaggregated evidence.
They should report only the measure that improved most.

questions.explanation: The passage recognises their usefulness while identifying the limits of a single score.

questions.prompt: Which inference is best supported? (Passage: “A city index hides the distribution”)

options.text: Weights should be chosen only after the index is published.
A composite index can never compare outcomes over time.
The mayor’s strategy has definitely harmed informal workers.
A rise in the index does not alone establish that the strategy is fair or effective for every group.

questions.explanation: A better score measures movement in selected indicators, not a complete policy verdict.

questions.prompt: Which assumption does the agency make when it equates boardings with improved employment access? (Passage: “The railway station is not the whole journey”)

options.text: Additional rail use translates into more convenient journeys to places where jobs are available.
Every passenger boards at the same station.
Employment locations never change.
Passenger counts are too costly to collect.

questions.explanation: The conclusion assumes station activity represents the broader door-to-door outcome.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most directly test the agency’s claim? (Passage: “The railway station is not the whole journey”)

options.text: The number of posters displayed inside stations.
Door-to-door travel times and the connection between stations and employment locations.
The total length of railway track in the country.
The number of train drivers employed by the agency.

questions.prompt: Which alternative explanation for rising boardings is identified? (Passage: “The railway station is not the whole journey”)

options.text: A rise in boardings proves that all commuters have faster journeys.
A decrease in feeder-bus services necessarily increases accessibility.
Population growth or a fare discount may increase use without proving improved job access.
A temporary event cannot affect passenger counts.

questions.prompt: Which finding would most weaken the employment-access claim? (Passage: “The railway station is not the whole journey”)

options.text: Household surveys show shorter door-to-door commutes.
Feeder buses become more frequent and reliable.
New stations are built near industrial employment clusters.
Boardings rise, but transfer delays make total journeys to major job centres longer.

questions.prompt: What does the passage concede about passenger counts? (Passage: “The railway station is not the whole journey”)

options.text: They are objective, inexpensive and useful for tracking demand over time.
They are useless for every transport decision.
They independently establish the quality of all journeys.
They measure the safety of every feeder route.

questions.explanation: The text acknowledges the measure’s strengths while limiting the conclusion drawn from it.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported? (Passage: “The railway station is not the whole journey”)

options.text: Passenger growth always reflects a fare discount.
The service may attract more riders without necessarily improving access to employment.
A rail service should be judged only by employment outcomes.
Low passenger use always proves that a station is inaccessible.

questions.explanation: The final paragraph separates increased use from the broader outcome of employment access.

questions.prompt: Which flaw most directly affects the department’s causal conclusion? (Passage: “A laboratory’s result needs a comparison group”)

options.text: The department measured attendance over three months.
The clinics used text messages rather than printed letters.
The before-and-after comparison does not rule out other changes that could explain higher attendance.
The reminder system was introduced by a health department.

options.text: Ask clinic managers whether they believe the system is successful.
Compare pilot clinics with the largest hospital in another State.
Count only the number of messages sent by the vendor.
Compare similar clinics over the same period, checking pre-pilot trends and relevant differences.

questions.prompt: Why record undelivered messages and households without reliable phones? (Passage: “A laboratory’s result needs a comparison group”)

options.text: To determine whether the intervention reaches groups equally and identify gaps in access.
To prove that every patient owns a mobile phone.
To avoid measuring completed vaccinations.
To show that privacy protections are unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Which outcome is a better measure of the programme’s health objective? (Passage: “A laboratory’s result needs a comparison group”)

options.text: The number of reminder messages drafted.
Completed vaccination with the correct dose, rather than clinic arrival alone.
The number of clinics displaying the pilot logo.
The total number of staff meetings held.

options.text: The clinics had comparable pre-pilot attendance trends.
Undelivered messages were tracked accurately.
A separate outreach campaign began at the same clinics during the same period and likely increased attendance.

options.text: Replace all clinic services with automated messages.
Abandon text reminders because they cannot be evaluated.
Extend the system immediately because attendance rose.
Treat the result as promising but test causation, completion and equitable reach before scaling.

₹18 crore

₹9.6 crore

₹10.44 crore
₹12.72 crore
₹11.4 crore

questions.prompt: How many patients can be served in three full days? (Dataset: “A mobile health outreach schedule”)
questions.explanation: Three full days at 48 patients per day give 3 × 48 = 144.

questions.prompt: How many patients are allocated to village A under the stated full-day share? (Dataset: “A mobile health outreach schedule”)
questions.explanation: Village A receives 25% of the 48-patient full-day capacity: 0.25 × 48 = 12 patients.

questions.prompt: How many patients can be seen during the final half-day? (Dataset: “A mobile health outreach schedule”)
questions.explanation: The dataset states that the final half-day is planned for 30 follow-up visits.

questions.prompt: If the half-day follow-up list has 24 patients, what proportion of its capacity remains unused? (Dataset: “A mobile health outreach schedule”)
questions.explanation: Unused capacity is 30 − 24 = 6 places. The unused share is 6 ÷ 30 × 100 = 20%.

questions.prompt: How many containers received both checks? (Dataset: “A port's container inspection data”)
questions.explanation: The remaining share is 25%; 25% of 1,200 = 300.

questions.prompt: How many documentary-only containers were cleared on the same day? (Dataset: “A port's container inspection data”)
questions.explanation: The documentary-only group is 45% of 1,200 = 540 containers. Of these, 80% are cleared: 0.80 × 540 = 432.

questions.prompt: How many physical-only containers were not cleared on the same day? (Dataset: “A port's container inspection data”)
questions.explanation: The physical-only group is 30% of 1,200 = 360 containers. Since 65% are cleared, 35% are not: 0.35 × 360 = 126.

questions.prompt: What was the total number cleared on the same day across the three groups? (Dataset: “A port's container inspection data”)
questions.explanation: Same-day clearances total 432 documentary-only + 234 physical-only (65% of 360) + 120 combined-check containers = 786.
